title: India Overhauls NTA Leadership and Appoints Reform Panel as NEET Crisis Deepens
excerpt: Two new joint secretaries have been installed at the scandal-hit National Testing Agency, while a seven-member committee led by former ISRO chief K. Radhakrishnan has been tasked with fixing the broken examination system before the June 21 re-exam.
body:
The Indian government has moved to overhaul the leadership of the National Testing Agency, appointing Ruchita Vij and Anuja Bapat as joint secretaries with immediate effect and installing a seven-member reform committee to redesign the country's examination infrastructure — the clearest sign yet that New Delhi views the NEET-UG paper leak scandal as a systemic crisis, not an isolated breach.

The appointments come as the CBI investigation into the leak accelerates, with the arrest of what investigators have described as the "kingpin" — a chemistry professor from Pune — and as a doctors' professional body has filed a plea in the Supreme Court demanding the outright dissolution of the NTA.

The Scale of the Crisis

The NEET-UG 2026 examination, taken by roughly 2.4 million aspiring medical students across India, was scrapped in May after evidence emerged that the question paper had been leaked and circulated before the test. The cancellation — the first of its kind for a national medical entrance exam — triggered protests across the country, with students and parents describing years of preparation rendered meaningless by institutional failure.

The government subsequently announced a re-examination on June 21, but the credibility of the NTA, which was established in 2017 to professionalise India's high-stakes testing infrastructure, has been severely damaged. This is not the agency's first controversy: the UGC-NET exam was also compromised in a separate leak incident, prompting the formation of the Radhakrishnan committee to examine both failures.

What the Reform Panel Will Do

The committee, led by Dr. K. Radhakrishnan — former chairman of the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) — has been tasked with reviewing NTA's operational processes, data security protocols, question paper handling procedures and examination logistics. The panel's mandate covers:

  • Transparency in exam design and distribution
  • Data security at every stage of the paper lifecycle
  • Technology upgrades to prevent leaks during printing, transport and storage
  • Institutional governance reforms within NTA itself

The committee is expected to deliver recommendations before the June 21 re-exam, though observers are sceptical that meaningful structural changes can be implemented in barely five weeks.

A System Under Strain

India's examination system processes tens of millions of candidates annually across NEET, JEE (for engineering), CUET (for university admissions) and dozens of state-level tests. The centralisation of these exams under the NTA was originally intended to reduce corruption and standardise quality — but critics now argue the agency has become a single point of failure, with neither the security infrastructure nor the institutional culture to match its enormous mandate.

The Pune professor's arrest suggests an organised network, not a lone actor. CBI investigators are reportedly examining links between coaching centres, exam logistics contractors and individuals with access to question papers — a supply chain of corruption that mirrors patterns seen in earlier exam scandals at the state level.

What NRI Families Should Know

The NEET crisis has direct implications for the hundreds of thousands of NRI families whose children aspire to study medicine in India. Many students in the US, UK, Canada and the Gulf states prepare for NEET while attending school abroad, often enrolling in expensive coaching programmes. The June 21 re-exam date means disrupted summer schedules, additional travel costs for those who need to sit the exam in India, and lingering uncertainty about whether the re-examination itself will be secure.

Parents in diaspora communities have been particularly vocal on social media, with many questioning whether the NTA can be trusted to administer a fair exam without fundamental reform.

What's Next

The Radhakrishnan committee's recommendations, the CBI's ongoing investigation and the Supreme Court's response to the dissolution plea will all shape the path forward. For now, the June 21 date stands — but with the NTA's credibility in tatters and public trust at a historic low, the government faces the challenge of not just re-running an exam but rebuilding the institution that administers it.
author: Diaspora Desk
